data.title: Missing Operating System Security Updates
data.summary:
Systems within the environment were missing security updates addressing
vulnerabilities for which reliable public exploit code exists, allowing remote
compromise without credentials.
data.description:
Hosts were identified running operating system builds that had not received
security updates released by the vendor. The absent updates addressed
vulnerabilities in network-facing services, several of which permit code
execution prior to authentication.

Exploit code for these vulnerabilities is publicly available, integrated into
widely distributed exploitation frameworks, and requires no specialist knowledge
to use. The interval between a patch being published and exploit code appearing
is routinely measured in days, so the exposure period represented by an unpatched
host is substantial.

Exploitation of the affected services typically yields execution in the context
of the operating system kernel or a highly privileged service account, meaning
successful exploitation results in immediate and complete compromise of the host
rather than a limited foothold requiring further escalation.

Affected systems were identified through service version
enumeration and confirmed where testing could be conducted safely.
data.impact:
An attacker with network access to the affected systems could obtain complete
control of them without any credentials, using publicly available tooling. This
grants access to all data held on those hosts, permits the extraction of
credential material from memory including that of privileged users who have
logged on, and provides a position from which the remainder of the network can be
attacked.
data.recommendation:
1. Apply all outstanding security updates to the affected systems as a
   priority, beginning with those addressing vulnerabilities in network-facing
   services that permit unauthenticated code execution.

2. Where a system cannot be patched within a reasonable period due to application
   compatibility, isolate it at the network level so that the affected services
   are reachable only from systems that genuinely require access, and document
   the exception with a review date.

3. Implement a patch management process with defined timescales by severity, and
   report against those timescales so that exceptions are visible to management
   rather than accumulating silently.

4. Deploy vulnerability scanning across the estate on a recurring basis and
   reconcile the results against the asset inventory, so that systems missing
   from patch management are identified.

5. Review the asset inventory itself, as unpatched systems are frequently those
   that no team recognises as their responsibility.
